title: THE UNTOLD MYSTERY OF THE GIANT EGYPTIAN KILLED BY BENAIAH WITH HIS OWN SPEAR
paragraphs: THE UNTOLD MYSTERY OF THE GIANT EGYPTIAN KILLED BY BENAIAH WITH HIS OWN SPEAR
The warrior was enormous.
His weapon was terrifying.
His reputation was enough to make ordinary men reconsider the fight before it even began.
And yet history barely remembers his name.
Instead, Scripture preserves the name of the man who walked toward him.
Benaiah.
A warrior whose story is often overshadowed by David, yet whose faith-filled courage contains one of the most astonishing victories recorded in the Bible.
It happened in only a few verses.
But hidden inside those verses is a profound mystery about spiritual warfare, divine courage, and how God often defeats giants using the very weapons they trusted to protect themselves.
Most people know about David and Goliath.
Few know about Benaiah and the Egyptian.
Even fewer understand why this battle was preserved in Scripture.
And almost nobody realizes how deeply this story reaches into our own lives today.
Because every believer eventually faces an Egyptian.
Not merely a person.
A giant.
A fear.
A stronghold.
A voice that appears bigger than God's promise.
The account appears in 2 Samuel 23:20-21 and again in 1 Chronicles 11:22-23.
The text says:

"Benaiah son of Jehoiada was a valiant warrior from Kabzeel, who performed great exploits. He struck down two sons of Ariel of Moab. He also went down into a pit on a snowy day and killed a lion. And he struck down an Egyptian, a handsome man. The Egyptian had a spear in his hand like a weaver's beam, but Benaiah went down to him with a club. He snatched the spear from the Egyptian's hand and killed him with his own spear."
At first glance, it seems like a brief military achievement.
But Scripture rarely wastes words.
Every detail matters.
Every detail is there for a reason.
The Hebrew text calls Benaiah a "ben ish chayil."
חַיִל (chayil)
This word means strength, valor, capability, excellence, power, and proven character.
This was not merely a strong soldier.
This was a man forged through testing.
A man whose courage had already survived battles nobody else wanted.
That matters because courage is never born in public.
It is developed in hidden places.
Long before Benaiah faced the Egyptian giant, he had already descended into a snowy pit to fight a lion.
Most people avoid lions.
Most people avoid pits.
Most people avoid snow-covered pits containing lions.
Benaiah entered one.
Voluntarily.
Faith had already taught him to move toward danger when God was with him.
Then comes the giant Egyptian.
The Hebrew description reveals an intimidating figure.
The Egyptian carried a spear "like a weaver's beam."
The same phrase appears in descriptions of Goliath.
The image is intentional.
The Bible wants us to see another giant.
Another impossible battle.
Another moment where fear should have won.
Yet something remarkable happens.
Benaiah does not possess equal weaponry.
He is outmatched.
Outarmed.
Outsized.
The giant has a spear.
Benaiah has a club.
From a military perspective, this is absurd.
From a spiritual perspective, this is often exactly how God works.
Again and again throughout Scripture, God places His servants in situations where natural calculations fail.
Moses had a staff.
David had a sling.
Shamgar had an oxgoad.
Samson had a donkey's jawbone.
And Benaiah had a club.
The pattern is unmistakable.
God delights in demonstrating that victory never originates from human superiority.
Victory originates from divine presence.
One of the most fascinating details appears in the Hebrew verb describing what Benaiah did.
He "snatched" the spear.
The word conveys forceful seizure.
Decisive action.
Aggressive courage.
He did not merely defend himself.
He advanced.
He closed the distance.
He entered the giant's space.
He took control of the very thing designed to kill him.
Then came the shocking conclusion.
The giant died by his own spear.
This is where the story transforms from military history into spiritual revelation.
Throughout Scripture, God repeatedly causes evil to collapse under its own weight.
Haman builds gallows and hangs on them.
Daniel's accusers enter the lions' den they intended for him.
Pharaoh's army drowns in the sea they thought would trap Israel.
The enemy's weapon becomes the enemy's downfall.
What appears powerful becomes powerless.
What appears invincible becomes vulnerable.
What appears unstoppable collapses.
The giant trusted the spear.
The spear became his destruction.
The mystery runs even deeper.
When the Greek translators of the Old Testament rendered these narratives centuries before Christ, they preserved the theme of decisive divine reversal.
This theme reaches its climax at the cross.
Satan believed he had won.
The religious leaders believed Jesus was defeated.
Rome believed another rebel had been crushed.
Yet the very instrument intended to destroy Christ became the instrument through which salvation entered the world.
The cross became victory.
The grave became resurrection.
Death became life.
The enemy's weapon became the means of God's triumph.
This pattern echoes throughout redemption history.
It is one of God's signatures.
And perhaps that is why Benaiah's story was preserved.
Not merely because a giant died.
But because God was revealing how He works.
There is another mystery hidden in Benaiah's name.
His name comes from the Hebrew:
בְּנָיָהוּ
Bena-yahu
Meaning:
"Yahweh has built."
Or:
"Built by the LORD."
What a remarkable contrast.
The giant trusted what he carried.
Benaiah trusted Who had built him.
One relied on weaponry.
The other relied on formation.
One trusted size.
The other trusted God.
And that distinction changes everything.
Many believers spend years praying for bigger weapons.
God often spends those years building bigger warriors.
We ask God to remove battles.
He asks us to become stronger through them.
We ask for easier paths.
He develops deeper faith.
We ask for fewer giants.
He develops giant-killers.
The world celebrates visible strength.
God develops invisible strength.
The world admires weapons.
God shapes character.
The world chases appearance.
God builds substance.
Benaiah's victory was not created on the battlefield.
It was revealed there.
The battle exposed what God had already built.
And perhaps that is the message someone reading this desperately needs today.
Your giant may not carry a spear.
It may be depression.
Fear.
Addiction.
Regret.
Financial collapse.
A broken marriage.
A secret struggle nobody knows about.
A diagnosis that stole your sleep.
A burden that follows you everywhere.
And every day it whispers the same lie:
"You are not enough."
On your own, that may be true.
But Benaiah's story was never about what Benaiah possessed.
It was about what God had built inside him.
The same God who strengthened David.
The same God who strengthened Benaiah.
The same God who raised Jesus from the dead.
The same God is still transforming lives today.
The Greek New Testament uses the word δύναμις (dynamis) to describe God's power.
Not human strength.
Divine power.
Supernatural enablement.
The power that accomplishes what human ability never could.
The Gospel is not the story of strong people succeeding.
It is the story of God empowering weak people who trust Him.
That is why Benaiah still matters.
Because his story points beyond himself.
Beyond David.
Beyond Israel.
Beyond military victories.
Ultimately, it points toward Jesus Christ.
The greater Giant-Slayer.
The One who faced humanity's greatest enemies: sin, death, and Satan.
The One who conquered not with earthly weapons but through perfect obedience and sacrificial love.
The One who transformed defeat into victory.
The One who still rescues sinners today.
Maybe that is why this forgotten battle remains unforgettable.
Because deep down we all know what it feels like to stand before something larger than ourselves.
And we all need the reminder that giants are not measured by their size.
They are measured by God's sovereignty over them.
The Egyptian giant looked impossible.
Then God wrote the final sentence.
Your giant is not holding the pen either.
Your testimony may strengthen someone reading these words in silence.
And remember this:
The giant never realized that the weapon he trusted most would become the instrument of his defeat.
